title: From Mixture of Experts to Mixture of Agents with Super Fast Inference - Daniel Kim & Daria Soboleva

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The workshop's core activity is building and configuring a Mixture of Agents system with layered multi-agent architecture, planning, critique, and summarization agents. MoA is a general-purpose multi-agent architecture pattern demonstrated across coding and math problem domains without a specific application vertical. The workshop covers both development of MoA applications and deployment on Cerebras inference infrastructure. Requires API setup, GitHub fork, and hands-on coding with model and agent configuration, but includes introductory MoE explanations. Hands-on workshop with live demos, a competitive coding challenge, and extended Q&A. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript.

summary: The workshop begins with introductions. Daria Soboleva, Head Research Scientist at Cerebras for 4.5 years, focuses on MoE architectures and hardware-efficient training; she created SlimPajama and previously worked at Google. Daniel Kim is Head of Growth at Cerebras. Daria traces LLM evolution from GPT-3 through DeepSeek 3 and explains MoE: the transformer's feed-forward network is a bottleneck, so MoE replaces it with multiple specialized expert networks plus a router selecting which expert to use per token. Daniel introduces inference-time compute and the data wall, demonstrating with an AIME math problem where GPT-4o took 45 seconds (wrong answer) and GPT-o3 took 293 seconds (correct answer). He then introduces MoA as leveraging collective intelligence of multiple LLMs with custom system prompts. NinjaTech AI solved the same AIME problem in 7.4 seconds using MoA on Cerebras—500,000+ tokens across 32 LLM calls. Cerebras' speed advantage comes from 900,000 cores with 900,000 individual 1:1 memory stores on-chip. The hands-on workshop uses a Streamlit app with layered agent architecture. A competitive coding challenge requires configuring MoA to generate a Python function scoring 120 points; multiple attendees achieved perfect scores. Extended Q&A covers Cerebras data center expansion (6 US centers, France this year, Canada planned), power consumption (~1/3 of Nvidia GPUs), model onboarding speed (dependent on kernel availability—Qwen 32B was quick due to Llama architecture similarity), custom architecture support via partnerships (Mistral example), enterprise fine-tuned model support (LoRA on roadmap), diffusion models (still in research but an internal demo was promising), multimodal APIs (released through Mistral app, coming to public cloud), and Cerebras advantages for unstructured sparsity algorithms. Daria notes Cerebras is working with model companies to design models specifically optimized for current and future Cerebras chip generations. The best inference use case is serving very large models, as Cerebras scales linearly across chips without the overhead of distributing model weights. There is no hard limit to model size—Cerebras can serve models from 8 billion parameters up to Maverick, with plans for larger Meta models. The public API uses a shared pool with per-user rate limits, and Cerebras handles backend provisioning automatically; users cannot partition a single instance. Daniel emphasizes MoA performance depends heavily on prompt quality and configuration engineering. Daria notes the theoretical basis in ensemble learning and warns that too many agents create redundancy without contributing to the final solution. Daniel closes by inviting startups to discuss inference needs and asking coding challenge winners to bring proof of their 120-point scores for prizes.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Bios
sections.summary: Daria introduces herself as Head Research Scientist at Cerebras focusing on MoE and hardware-efficient training; she created SlimPajama and previously worked at Google. Daniel introduces himself as Head of Growth handling developer activations and startup token distribution. He highlights intern Kevin, a high school student who built most of the workshop. Daniel asks the audience about Cerebras awareness and previews the company's custom silicon advantage.

sections.title: Cerebras Hardware and Inference Speed
sections.summary: Daniel explains Cerebras makes custom silicon for fast AI inference, showing a side-by-side chip comparison with Nvidia H100. Cerebras holds world records for every publicly hosted model, approximately 15.5x faster than the fastest GPU provider for Llama 3.3 70B. He positions Cerebras as the only option for significantly faster inference.

sections.title: LLM Evolution and the Need for MoE
sections.summary: Daria traces LLM evolution: GPT-3 showed scaling improves performance; Llama emphasized data curation and token count; DeepSeek 3 at 600B parameters required architectural innovations. She frames MoE as the answer to scaling model parameters efficiently for both training and inference.

sections.title: Mixture of Experts Architecture Explained
sections.summary: Daria explains that the feed-forward network in a transformer is a bottleneck because it must disentangle information from attention layers and decide which neurons to activate for diverse tasks. MoE replaces the monolithic feed-forward network with multiple specialized expert networks plus a router that selects which expert to use per token. This increases model capacity without increasing inference time, and is the industry standard used by OpenAI, Anthropic, and others.

sections.title: Inference-Time Compute and Reasoning Models
sections.summary: Daniel introduces inference-time compute, referencing Ilya Sutskever's observation about the impending data wall. He demonstrates with an AIME math problem: GPT-4o (non-reasoning) took 45 seconds to produce a wrong answer, while GPT-o3 (reasoning) took 293 seconds to produce the correct answer, highlighting the tradeoff between reasoning quality and latency.

sections.title: Mixture of Agents Introduction and NinjaTech AI Demo
sections.summary: Daniel introduces Mixture of Agents as leveraging collective intelligence of multiple LLMs—sending inputs to multiple models with custom system prompts, then combining responses via a final model. Together AI coined the term and benchmarked it as outperforming frontier models. Daniel shows NinjaTech AI solving the same AIME problem in 7.4 seconds using MoA on Cerebras, using a planning agent, critique agent, iteration, and summarization agent—500,000+ tokens across 32 LLM calls.

sections.title: Cerebras Hardware Architecture Deep Dive
sections.summary: Daniel explains why Cerebras is faster: the H100 GPU has ~17,000 cores but stores weights and KV cache off-chip, creating memory channel bottlenecks as models grow. Cerebras has 900,000 cores with 900,000 individual 1:1 memory stores on-chip, eliminating memory transfer delays. Cerebras scales linearly—only activations transfer between chips via a single Ethernet cord.

sections.title: MoA Benefits and Workshop Setup
sections.summary: Daria frames MoA as enabling zero-shot problem solving by specializing each agent for a problem portion, using a surgery analogy. The hands-on workshop begins: attendees need a Cerebras API key, star and fork a GitHub repo, and deploy via Streamlit or locally. Kevin accidentally committed his API key to the repo, providing a humorous moment.

sections.title: MoA App UI Walkthrough and Non-Competitive Demo
sections.summary: Daniel walks through the Streamlit MoA app UI: a summarization agent at the top aggregates results, and agent management allows creating individual agents with custom prompts, temperature, model selection, and naming. Layers are sequential but agents within each layer process in parallel; each layer's concatenated output serves as input for the next. Attendees ask fun questions like planning a San Francisco trip.

sections.title: Competitive Coding Challenge
sections.summary: Daniel introduces a competitive challenge: configure a MoA system to generate a Python function called calculate_user_matrix that scores 120 points in an automated grader. Three preset agents address bugs/edge cases, performance optimization, and overall aggregation. Changing the main agent model to Qwen improved the score from C to B. Daria and the intern both achieved perfect scores.

sections.title: Challenge Winners and Q&A Begins
sections.summary: Multiple attendees raise hands confirming they achieved perfect 120 scores. Q&A begins with an audience question about AutoML for MoA—automating prompt engineering for harder problems. Daniel references Devin as an example of automated code generation already happening, emphasizing Cerebras aims to make such workflows faster.

sections.title: Q&A: Data Centers, Model Onboarding, and Power Consumption
sections.summary: Daniel explains Cerebras opened 6 data centers in the US in the last year, with one in France this year and one planned in Canada, expecting continued global expansion. On model onboarding, he says it depends on kernel availability: Qwen 32B was quick because its architecture was similar to Llama's, while novel architectures require custom kernel engineering. On power consumption, Cerebras uses approximately 1/3 the power of Nvidia GPUs for equivalent inference workloads, though the comparison isn't apples-to-apples due to different chip architectures and Cerebras's larger throughput per system.

sections.title: Q&A: MoA Benchmarking, Ensemble Theory, and Agent Redundancy
sections.summary: An audience member asks about MoA benchmarks versus other models. Daniel emphasizes MoA performance depends heavily on prompt quality—poor prompts yield poor results—and it requires engineering effort to optimize the system, not just out-of-the-box deployment. Daria notes the theoretical basis in ensemble learning: multiple models communicating can provide more robust, generalized solutions, similar to XGBoost or decision trees. When asked if too many agents could create worse solutions, Daria explains that excessive agents create redundancy—not all will be used in the final solution, wasting compute time, analogous to feature importance in boosting.

sections.title: Q&A: Fine-Tuned Models, Diffusion Models, and Custom Architectures
sections.summary: Daniel confirms enterprise clients can run custom fine-tuned models; LoRA fine-tuned model support is on the roadmap but not yet publicly available. On diffusion text generation models, Daria says they're still in research with no proven training recipe, but Daniel reveals he saw an internal demo that was 'insane' though he can't discuss details. On custom architectures, Daniel cites Mistral as a partnership example where their engineers and Cerebras engineers collaborated to create supporting kernels. He notes Cerebras hardware is fundamentally memory and compute organized efficiently, so it can theoretically support diverse architectures.

sections.title: Q&A: Multimodal, Real-Time APIs, and Hardware-Specific Models
sections.summary: Daniel reveals Cerebras released its first multimodal API through the Mistral app for image-based queries, with plans to scale to public cloud soon. Real-time APIs are being considered given Cerebras's inference speed advantage. When asked about models engineered specifically for Cerebras hardware, Daria highlights advantages for unstructured sparsity algorithms for pre-training, noting GPU performance would struggle with these. For inference, the product is only ~9 months old, and Cerebras is working with frontier model companies like Mistral to expand capabilities.

sections.title: Q&A: Model Scaling, Instance Sizing, and Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Daria explains Cerebras is working with model companies to design models specifically optimized for current and future chip generations. The best inference use case is serving very large models, as Cerebras scales linearly across multiple chips without the overhead of distributing model weights. There is no hard limit to model size—ranging from 8B parameters up to Maverick, with plans for larger Meta models—though costs scale with chip count. Users cannot partition a single SOC instance; Cerebras handles backend provisioning automatically via a shared API pool with per-user rate limits. Daniel closes by inviting startups to discuss inference needs and asking coding challenge winners to bring proof of 120-point scores for prizes.
